workload: Indemnity claims adjudication runs as several dependent stages: pull the claim data off the submitted documents, validate it against the group certificate in force on the date of service, cross-check the diagnosis codes against the member's own claim history, then route anything flagged to a reviewer. The certificate that governs a claim is itself the hard part — the version in the system may have been superseded by a change request that was never applied. A run that dies halfway through must not redo the stages that already completed, and every figure a reviewer sees has to trace back to the document it came from.

Total-loss motor claims move through four sub-processes end to end: intake of the adjuster paperwork and valuation reports, a settlement calculation, a lienholder and title check, and a payout authorisation that a human signs. Each stage produces evidence the next stage depends on, some stages wait on external parties for days, and an exception at any point has to park the file without losing the work already done.

Policy binders and freedom-of-service sheets feed our booking systems across three regions and nineteen lines of business. The pipeline orchestrates the whole booking end to end, and the binders themselves are not uniform — the aviation ones list fifteen to twenty aircraft each, which is where our current extraction stops returning everything. Booking cannot complete until the governing schedule for each line is resolved, and part-completed runs have to resume rather than restart.

Our clinical specialists bookmark the pages of a patient chart that matter for a prior-authorisation submission and mark the item ready. An agent then needs to read only those bookmarked pages and answer the payer's clinical questions in its own words. There is no field set to capture and no correction workflow — the specialist stays responsible for what gets submitted, and the agent is only reading the evidence they already selected.

When an instrument run fails, a technician attaches the vendor's diagnostic dump — a few pages of mixed text and tables, different for every manufacturer — to the ticket. We want the agent to read that attachment and say in plain language what the instrument was complaining about, so the technician can decide whether to recalibrate or call the vendor. A handful a day. Nobody is measuring field accuracy and there is nothing downstream that consumes a structured result.

Small-grant applications come in with one or two supporting attachments — a budget sheet, sometimes a letter of support. Before a panel member spends time on an application we want an agent to read the attachments and say whether they contain enough to assess it, recommending proceed, return to applicant, or send to a human. It is not capturing the budget numbers; a panel member still decides, and anything unreadable should send the application to a person rather than be guessed at.

Quote requests arrive in a shared mailbox, around a hundred thousand a year across eight countries. The request details might be in the email body, in one attachment, or spread across several where only one is the actual request and the rest are supporting material. A good number of the messages are not quote requests at all. Before anything can be captured we have to decide, per message, whether this is a request and which part of it carries it.

Complaints reach us through twelve channels — email, web forms, a legacy messaging system, physical mail — and every one of them has to be sorted into one of seventy-seven categories before a case is opened. Getting the category wrong sends the complaint to the wrong team and restarts the clock. We need the category decided and the case routed; the case record itself gets built afterwards.

For each flagged patient account we read the payer correspondence sitting in our imaging system and decide whether it is a genuine denial, and if so which denial reason applies. Calling a denial when there is not one sends the account down an appeals path that costs weeks. On a blind set we found that pushing critical errors to zero left only about a fifth of volume running untouched, while a looser threshold ran most of it and let real errors through.

Enhanced due diligence on a single institutional client currently takes an analyst around thirty hours and we run about a thousand a year. The analyst works through a defined bundle — corporate registry filings, adverse media, prior reviews, transaction narratives — and produces one written assessment where every statement has to be traceable to the document behind it, including where two sources disagree. Turnaround matters less than the assessment holding up when it is challenged.

Before a regulator inspects a trial site, a quality manager has to work through that trial's document set and produce a written readiness assessment — what is in order, what is missing, and what would not survive a question. It has to cite the document behind every statement, and saying a requirement is met has to mean the whole set was looked at, not that a matching document turned up.

After a major outage we collect everything: the paging timeline, chat transcripts, change records, vendor status pages, and the on-call engineers' own notes. Someone has to turn that fixed pile into one written post-incident report with a defensible sequence of events, calling out where two sources contradict each other and citing which record supports each claim. The collection is already done and somebody else signs the report off.

Our operations teams keep asking the same kinds of questions about internal standard operating procedures — which approval a given transaction needs, what the cut-off is, which form applies. The SOP library is maintained centrally and reused by everyone; a typical question is settled by one procedure. Live transaction status comes from the operational system, not from the SOPs.

Underwriters need to look up what our own underwriting manual says about a specific risk class. The manual is versioned, the current edition is the one indexed, and the answer is normally a single section they then apply themselves. They want the passage and its edition, not a recommendation — and if the manual genuinely does not address the risk they need to be told that rather than handed the nearest paragraph.

Our tariff documentation is maintained separately per operating region, and the same term — say, a demurrage free period — means different things region to region. An agent has to answer a definition or procedure question inside one named region and cite the regional document it came from, without blending in another region's wording.

Every inbound invoice has to be resolved to a company code and then to a vendor, and the two are dependent: which vendor records are even candidates depends on which company code the first step landed on. The reference sets are large — thousands of locations, millions of vendor records — and the names on invoices are noisy, abbreviated and inconsistently punctuated, so an exact key match fails most of the time. Where the second step cannot be confirmed the invoice should come back unresolved rather than matched to the closest-looking vendor.

We have pension participants whose mail keeps bouncing. Tracing one means starting from the plan record, following whatever identifiers that turns up into other sources, and using what comes back to decide where to look next — an employer record leads to a payroll reference, which leads somewhere else again. Where the chain cannot be completed the participant stays flagged as untraced rather than being assigned a best-guess address.

When a new sanctions measure lands, an analyst has to work out which of our internal control standards it touches. The measure names an authority and a legal instrument; finding the affected standards means looking that instrument up, taking the control references it cites, and chasing those into the standards library, where the wording rarely matches. Each lookup tells you what the next one should be, and anything that cannot be tied back to a cited control is raised as a question rather than assumed.

Supplier invoices from around two thousand suppliers across five countries arrive in widely varying formats, and we need the same thirty-odd fields off every one of them to post into the finance system. Low-confidence fields have to go to a validation step before anything posts, and a wrong value that gets through becomes a payment error, so per-field accuracy and the correction workflow are both hard requirements.

On a death notification we pull the beneficiary details off the policy documentation and cross-check the beneficiary change request against the confirmation letter that acknowledged it. The documents are already sorted by type before we get to them. A wrong beneficiary is the worst outcome we have, so every field goes through validation before a payment is set up, and an unreadable value has to stay unresolved rather than be filled in.

Before a clinician can be placed we verify around seventy-eight requirement types off ten document types — licences, certifications, screening results — running to tens of thousands of checks a month. Each document type has its own fixed field set, the documents are already separated by type, and a missed expiry date places someone who should not be working, so per-field review is mandatory.

Around a hundred thousand trade-deduction claims a year land as rows in a table, each with a short free-text reason a customer's clerk typed — shorthand, abbreviations, sometimes a promotion name. We need a normalised deduction reason code appended to every row, drawn from a fixed list, so the rows can be matched to agreements afterwards. Nothing about one row depends on another, and the matching and any system updates happen in later steps, not while reading the text.

We export a month of closed support tickets — tens of thousands of rows — and want two new columns on each: the root-cause category from a fixed list of about thirty, and a one-line plain-English summary of what actually went wrong. The free-text description is the only thing that carries it. Each ticket stands on its own, we are not calling anything out to another system, and the file goes to reporting afterwards.

Our product feed has thousands of rows where the structured attribute columns are blank but the seller-written description contains the answer — material, fit, intended use. We want those attributes filled per row from that description text, using a controlled vocabulary we already have, and rows where the description genuinely does not say should come back empty rather than guessed. One pass over the export, nothing looked up elsewhere.

A pricing engine gives us recommendations as JSON and the downstream system wants a CSV in a fixed column order, with a validation pass that rejects rows failing known rules and reports which ones failed. The mapping between the two formats is fully specified and does not change.

We screen our patient records for people likely eligible for a benefit programme who have not applied. The eligibility test is a defined set of rules over structured fields we already hold — income band, coverage status, length of condition — and the business wants to own and adjust those rules themselves.

Given a quarter of settled contract lines already in our warehouse, compute the rebate accrual per customer by applying each customer's tiered percentage to their qualifying volume, then produce the totals by region and by tier for the finance pack.
